documents.unit: BaylorITS and Office of the Provost
documents.title: Baylor's Generative AI Policy
documents.date_or_term: current; text from Wayback Machine capture (web.archive.org/web/2025/)
documents.stance_why: The page "embraces" AI yet says "Course instructors should specify the permitted use of AI tools", so it sets no course-level stance of its own and hands the decision to instructors.
documents.summary: Baylor's ITS and Provost page that sets nine guidelines for generative AI use and links resources and licensed tools. It welcomes AI but leaves permitted use in courses to instructors, with student misuse going to the Honor Council.

units.why: The opening sentence says Baylor "embraces Generative Artificial Intelligence as an effective tool", an institution-wide welcoming default, so it is a P02 stance statement addressed to all and informing rather than commanding.
units.anchor: Baylor embraces Generative Artificial Intelligence as an effective tool

units.why: The statement that "human conscience and intelligence are endowed by our Creator and cannot be replicated or replaced" sets a principle framing all AI use, so it fits the institution-wide framework type P56 rather than a stance type.
units.anchor: human conscience and intelligence are endowed by our Creator and cannot be replicated

units.why: "Existing university policies will apply to the use of AI to the greatest extent possible" is a scope principle that places AI under current rules, so it is a framework statement (P56) for all.
units.anchor: Existing university policies will apply to the use of AI to the greatest extent possible

units.why: "humans must retain the final decision-making authority" over employment, financial and mission-critical decisions is a human-in-the-loop rule for administrators; P46 covers only grades, so no listed type fits well.
units.anchor: humans must retain the final decision-making authority
units.frag_start: As AI-generated insights are increasingly used
units.frag_end: mission-critical decisions, humans must retain the final decision-making authority
units.uncovered_note: Humans keep final decision-making authority over AI-informed employment, financial and mission-critical decisions (not limited to grading).

units.why: New AI platforms and chatbots "must undergo review and approval by BaylorITS and the Office of the Provost before adoption", a pre-adoption approval gate; P65 is about contract and data-sharing review and P50 about preferring vetted tools, so neither matches an approval requirement for tools built in-house.
units.anchor: must undergo review and approval by BaylorITS and the Office of the Provost before adoption
units.frag_start: Any new generative AI platforms and chatbots
units.uncovered_note: New generative AI platforms and chatbots, including ones built by faculty, staff and students, need ITS and Provost review and approval before adoption.

units.why: "Use of AI tools in academic programs should be transparent" asks for openness about AI use in academics, which matches disclosure (P24); it is addressed to all and phrased as "should".
units.anchor: Use of AI tools in academic programs should be transparent
units.frag_start: Use of AI tools in academic programs

units.why: "Confidential data should be restricted for non-public AI tools" protects data going into tools, so it is P50 (protect data); it binds all users and says "should".
units.anchor: Confidential data should be restricted for non-public AI tools

units.why: "Actions resulting from AI tool usage are the sole responsibility of the user" makes users answerable for results and legal compliance, which is closest to P29 (own what you submit) though not limited to submissions.
units.anchor: Actions resulting from AI tool usage are the sole responsibility of the user

units.why: "AI policy violations will be addressed by the appropriate academic dean's office and the Office of the Provost" routes violations through administrative processes, so it is misconduct handling (P36) for admin.
units.anchor: AI policy violations will be addressed by the appropriate academic dean’s office

units.why: "Misuse of AI by students should be reported to the Honor Council and violations will be governed by the university's honor code" treats student AI misuse as honor-code misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Misuse of AI by students should be reported to the Honor Council
units.frag_end: governed by the university’s honor code.

units.why: "Course instructors should specify the permitted use of AI tools" leaves permission to each instructor, so it is P04 rather than P09 because it does not mention the syllabus; it binds instructors and says "should".
units.anchor: Course instructors should specify the permitted use of AI tools

units.why: The same sentence puts "the responsibilities of students to document what and how tools and data were used" on students, a documentation duty that fits P24 (disclose with submission); P26 needs full transcripts, which are not named.
units.anchor: responsibilities of students to document what and how tools and data were used
units.policy: Students document what and how AI tools and data were used in any course assignment.

units.why: "All AI-generated results must undergo human review to ensure accuracy" requires checking AI output, which is P31 (verify AI output); it applies to all users.
units.anchor: All AI-generated results must undergo human review to ensure accuracy

units.why: The research paragraph says AI tools can "summarize research content, analyze data ... or even operate as a research assistant", a statement of capability with no rule; no listed type covers descriptive capability claims, and P62 covers rules for research.
units.anchor: Current AI tools can summarize research content, analyze data
units.frag_start: Current AI tools can summarize research
units.uncovered_note: Descriptive statement that generative AI can accelerate research (summarize, analyze, hypothesize, review literature), with no rule attached.

units.why: "the research community must remain nimble and adjust to AI utilization methods quickly" says practice must keep changing as the technology changes, so it is P54 (revisit regularly).
units.anchor: the research community must remain nimble and adjust to AI utilization methods quickly
units.frag_start: These capabilities will expand and contract

units.why: The page lists "Microsoft Copilot Chat" among "Select Baylor-Licensed GenAI Platforms", offering a university-licensed tool, which is P17 (sanctioned tool).
units.anchor: Microsoft Copilot Chat is a GenAI tool used to query complex questions
units.frag_start: Microsoft Copilot Chat is a GenAI

units.why: The Instructor Guide is described as helping "instructors navigate the use of generative AI", a support resource for faculty (P63).
units.anchor: This guide is to help instructors navigate the use of generative AI.
units.frag_start: This guide is to help instructors

units.why: The Generative AI Literacy Course is "A Canvas-based course to get you up to speed on GenAI", a university offering that teaches AI use; closest is P44 (courses teach AI use), not a faculty-support type.
units.anchor: A Canvas-based course to get you up to speed on GenAI.

units.why: "Recommended Syllabus Statements" are offered to instructors so they can state AI expectations, matching P09 in spirit; the text only lists them (Box access required), hence informs.
units.anchor: Recommended Syllabus Statements

documents.title: Suggestions for Dealing with Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Produced Assignments
documents.date_or_term: current; text from Wayback Machine capture (web.archive.org/web/2025/)
documents.stance_why: It sets a baseline that submitting AI-produced work "as their own is not acceptable" but is a set of "suggestions" for faculty, leaving actual AI permissions to each instructor's expectations.
documents.summary: Office of Academic Integrity advice to faculty on essays produced by AI, with a Provost note that Turnitin AI detection was dropped. It recommends communicating expectations and redesigning assignments, and says passing off AI work as one's own violates the Honor Code.

units.why: The Provost update says the university will "allow the AI detection feature within Turnitin.com to expire" because of accuracy, which is a decision not to rely on detectors (P39).
units.anchor: allow the AI detection feature within Turnitin.com to expire at the end of December 2023
units.frag_start: the University has decided to allow

units.why: "Too much uncertainty exists, much of it related to accuracy" gives the stated reason for dropping detection; it supports P39 (detectors unreliable) and is separate from the decision itself.
units.anchor: Too much uncertainty exists, much of it related to accuracy
units.frag_start: Too much uncertainty exists, much of

units.why: Faculty are told to "Utilize the University's recommended syllabus statements", which pushes AI expectations into the syllabus (P09); addressed to instructors with a soft "may want to".
units.anchor: Utilize the University’s

units.why: Instructors should "Discuss this issue with students on the first day of class, communicate your expectations", a communication duty at course start; P09 is the nearest type though it is oral as well as syllabus.
units.anchor: Discuss this issue with students on the first day of class, communicate your expectations

units.why: Students are to be told that "submitting work produced by an AI system as their own is not acceptable", a ban on passing off AI work, which is P19.
units.anchor: submitting work produced by an AI system as their own is not acceptable
units.frag_start: Discuss this issue with students on

units.why: The same sentence calls such submission "a violation of Baylor's Honor Code", classifying it as misconduct (P36); the ban itself is coded as P19 in the previous unit.

units.why: "Familiarize yourself with AI systems. Try some of the essay prompts" tells faculty to learn the tools before designing, which is P63 (faculty learning AI).
units.anchor: Familiarize yourself with AI systems.

units.why: "Require writing to be done in class (by hand if possible)" moves writing to unassisted settings, matching P33 (shift to unassisted assessment).
units.anchor: Require writing to be done in class (by hand if possible).

units.why: Writing "essay prompts that are specific enough to other class assignments such that vague essays produced by AI systems won't be possible" redesigns assignments around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Write essay prompts that are specific enough to other class assignments
units.frag_start: Write essay prompts that are specific

units.why: "Consider incorporating personal reflections from students into essays" redesigns the assignment so AI is less useful, which is P35.
units.anchor: Consider incorporating personal reflections from students into essays where possible.

units.why: Incorporating "something about very recent events" exploits AI knowledge gaps in assignment design, so P35.
units.anchor: consider incorporating something about very recent events into essays
units.frag_start: AI systems appear not to be

units.why: "Require both in your essays, where possible, and then look for errors" requires citations and reference lists as an assignment design choice; I chose P35 over P40 because the instruction shapes the assignment, while the look-for-errors items are coded as P40.
units.anchor: Require both in your essays, where possible, and then look for errors.
units.frag_start: AI bots appear to struggle with

units.why: Requiring "multiple drafts of an essay (using ... a scaffolding approach)" restructures the assignment, which is P35; P26 concerns students keeping logs of AI use, which this is not.
units.anchor: Consider requiring students to submit multiple drafts of an essay
units.frag_start: Consider requiring students to submit multiple

units.why: Requiring a mix so "outside-of-class writing can be compared to his/her writing that is produced in class" uses comparison as evidence of misuse (P40) rather than a proctored shift (P33).
units.anchor: outside-of-class writing can be compared to his/her writing that is produced in class

units.why: "Incorporate a verbal exam requirement tied to an essay so that students are required to discuss what they are turning in" checks understanding orally (P34).
units.anchor: Incorporate a verbal exam requirement tied to an essay

units.why: "Look for vague general comparisons that tend to beg the question" gives signs of AI-written text to find misuse, so P40 (process evidence to identify misuse).

documents.title: Is using ChatGPT for coursework considered cheating?
documents.stance_why: The answer begins "It depends" and says "it’s up to each instructor to create policies", so it delegates, with one fixed limit on passing off ChatGPT writing as one's own.
documents.summary: A library FAQ telling students that whether ChatGPT use is cheating depends on each instructor. It adds that they should ask first and may never present an entirely ChatGPT-written paper as their own.

units.why: "it's up to each instructor to create policies for classroom use" hands the decision to instructors, so P04.
units.anchor: it’s up to each instructor to create policies for classroom use
units.frag_start: At Baylor University, it’s up to

units.why: "if your instructor doesn't allow it, it would be cheating" tells students unauthorized AI use counts as cheating, so P36.
units.anchor: if your instructor doesn’t allow it, it would be cheating

units.why: "many instructors do allow it for specific assignments or tasks" reports that permission varies by assignment, so P04.
units.anchor: many instructors do allow it for specific assignments or tasks

units.why: "Always ask your instructor what their policies are" is the ask-before-using rule, P10.
units.anchor: Always ask your instructor what their policies are.

units.why: "The best time to talk with your instructor is before you begin your assignment" sets timing for asking, a P10 point separate from the ask itself.
units.anchor: The best time to talk with your instructor is before you begin your assignment

units.why: "it's still against the principles of academic integrity to represent a paper entirely written by ChatGPT as your own" bans passing off AI-written work even where AI is allowed, which is P19.
units.anchor: against the principles of academic integrity to represent a paper entirely written by ChatGPT
units.frag_start: Even if your instructor does allow

notes: Text for the first two documents comes from Wayback captures. No school or computing-unit policy found; course syllabi deferred. Two UNCOVERED units (human final authority over AI-informed decisions; pre-adoption review of AI platforms) and one descriptive research-capability unit.
